title: How to Care for the Grieving
subtitle: Ministering to those who mourn with presence, the things never to say, and faithfulness through the long grief that outlasts the funeral

sections.title: The Table After Everyone Leaves
sections.body:
The funeral was full. The flowers were many. For two weeks the casseroles came and the cards arrived and the house was never empty. And then it all stopped, and the grieving woman sat down alone at her kitchen table in a silence she had never heard before.

That table is where grief actually lives. Not at the graveside. At the breakfast for one, three months later, when the world has moved on and she has not.

The church is usually present for the spectacle of grief and absent for its substance. We crowd the funeral and vanish from the long aftermath, because the funeral has a date and the aftermath does not. But grief does not keep the calendar's hours. It comes back in October when the leaves turn the way they did that year. It ambushes a man in the grocery aisle in front of a food his wife used to buy. To care for the grieving is to be there for that table, long after everyone else has decided the grieving should be done by now.

sections.title: Presence Before Words
sections.body:
The first ministry to the grieving is the same as the last. It is your presence, and the discipline to bring it without bringing answers.

The grieving do not need their loss explained. They need company in it. Job's friends were wise for exactly seven days, the days they sat in the dust and said nothing.

We rush to speak because the silence of another person's grief is unbearable to us, and so we fill it to comfort ourselves while telling ourselves we are comforting them. Resist that. Sit in the room. Let the silence be long. Weep with those who weep, which Scripture commands and which costs more than any sentence, because it means letting their pain reach you instead of holding it off with words. The most pastoral thing you may do all year is to be in a house, on a couch, doing nothing, saying nothing, and not leaving. The grieving will not remember your eloquence. They will remember that you came and that you stayed.

sections.title: The Things You Must Never Say
sections.body:
In the presence of fresh grief, the wrong sentence does damage that lasts for years, and almost every wrong sentence is reached for to relieve our own discomfort, not theirs.

Guard your mouth. The bereaved will remember what was said over that casket for the rest of their lives.

Do not say everything happens for a reason. Do not say God needed another angel, which is not even true. Do not say at least, the deadliest two words in the language of loss, because there is no at least at the foot of a grave, and the one who says it has just measured another person's agony and called it small. Do not say I know how you feel, because you do not, even if you have lost the same kind of person, because their loss is theirs and not yours. Do not hurry them toward a silver lining. What you can say is small and true. I am so sorry. I loved them too. You do not have to talk. I am not going anywhere. And then prove the last sentence by actually not going anywhere.

sections.title: Grief Is Longer Than You Think
sections.body:
We have a script that says grief lasts about a year, and the script is a lie that wounds people. Grief is not a process with a finish line. It is a changed shape a life takes around an absence.

The goal is not to get over it. The goal is to learn to carry it, and that learning takes years, not weeks.

The widower does not stop missing his wife in month thirteen. He misses her at the wedding she should have seen and the grandchild she never met and the ordinary Tuesday that arrives without her for the ten thousandth time. The cruelest thing the church does is signal, by its silence, that the grieving have taken too long. So mark the dates others forget. The anniversary of the death. The birthday. The first Christmas, and the fifth, which can be as hard as the first. A call on those days, a word that says I remembered, I have not forgotten them and I have not forgotten you. That is ministry to the long grief, and it is the part almost no one does, and it is the part that matters most.

sections.title: Hope That Does Not Hurry the Dark
sections.body:
We are tempted, as people of the resurrection, to rush the grieving toward the hope, to wave away the dark with the dawn we believe is coming. Do not.

The hope is real. It is the realest thing we have. But hope spoken too soon is not comfort. It is dismissal wearing the clothes of faith.

Jesus stood at the tomb of his friend, knowing he was minutes from raising him, and he wept anyway. He did not skip the grief because he knew the ending. He entered it. That is the model. We hold the resurrection and we hold the tears at the same time, and we refuse to use the first to silence the second. So sit in the dark with the grieving and do not turn on all the lights at once. Let them weep without correcting it. And when the hope is finally spoken, let it be gentle and let it be late, after the grief has been honored, the way a candle is lit in a room that has first been allowed to be dark. That is how you care for the grieving. Not by ending their night. By keeping watch in it with them until the morning that we trust is coming.
